title: Trump Sanctions ICC Hours After Its Former Judge Navi Pillay Wins Nobel Peace Prize
excerpt: The sweeping sanctions would cut the ICC off from US banks, insurers, and software providers — putting Washington on a collision course with eight allied nations that vowed to stand by the tribunal.
body:
• The Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, October 9, just hours after the court's former judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
  • The sanctions would ban transactions with the court, potentially cutting it off from US-based banks, insurers, software providers, and technology companies that keep it running.
  • The US Treasury issued a six-month wind-down waiver for American companies and individuals doing business with the court; the State Department said the window gives the court time to address US concerns.
  • The move triggered immediate backlash: the ICC called it an "assault on the rule of law," and the foreign ministers of eight allied nations — including Canada, Germany, France, Japan, and the UK — reaffirmed "continued and unwavering support" for the court.

Sanctions Hours After the Nobel

The timing could hardly have been more pointed. On Friday, October 9, the Norwegian Nobel Committee named Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, an 85-year-old South African jurist of Indian Tamil descent who served as a judge on the International Criminal Court's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. Hours later, the Trump administration announced it was sanctioning the very court she once served on.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=OBrVxEU-aHw

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the sanctions would ban transactions with what he called "this rogue court," arguing they would cut off the tribunal's resources and cripple its ability to operate. The measures go well beyond earlier US actions: where previous sanctions targeted individual prosecutors and judges, Friday's move hits the institution itself — potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court, from banking to insurance to software.

"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."

— Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State

A Nobel as a Rebuke

Pillay, born in Durban in 1941, defended anti-apartheid activists as a young lawyer, exposed the torture of political detainees, and became the first non-white woman to serve on South Africa's High Court. At the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish landmark precedents, including that rape and sexual violence could constitute crimes against humanity and genocide. She served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and, from 2021 to 2025, led a UN commission of inquiry whose September 2025 report concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The Nobel Committee said it chose Pillay to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack." It described the rule of law as an absolute necessity for peace, adding that "the judges — those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos — are therefore highly deserving of our praise."

Pillay was at a conference at the Nuremberg Court in Germany — the courtroom where the post-war Nazi trials laid the foundations of modern international law — when the prize was announced. "Is it true? I thought it must be a joke," she told the audience, according to CNN. She dedicated the award to survivors of international crimes and to those defending international criminal justice "whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign."

Why Washington Is Going After the Court

The Trump administration's hostility to the ICC is not new. It previously sanctioned ICC prosecutors and judges — moves first imposed during Trump's first term, rescinded under President Joe Biden, and revived within days of Trump's return to office in January 2025. The US objects to the court's jurisdiction over Americans and Israelis: Washington has never forgiven the ICC's past investigation of alleged US actions in Afghanistan, and it has been furious about the arrest warrants the court issued in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza. Neither the US nor Israel are parties to the court.

Several of the court's prosecutors have already been hit by US sanctions after the Netanyahu warrants. Court officials have been preparing for months for sanctions on the court itself, Reuters reported — shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance. Earlier this week, the court's registrar called on the EU to be ready to use a "blocking mechanism" shielding European entities from the sanctions' extraterritorial effects.

The Diplomatic Fallout

The response was swift. The ICC condemned the sanctions as an "assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order," vowing its work would continue. The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement saying they "regret and strongly disagree" with the US move and reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support" for the court. The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide, counts 125 member states, including every EU country and all NATO members except the United States and Turkey.

The Nobel Committee's implicit rebuke extended beyond Washington. Israel's foreign ministry reacted to Pillay's win with fury, accusing her of "lies" — a response rooted in the Gaza genocide findings her UN commission produced. Netanyahu said the committee had "lost its moral compass." Trump, who has openly campaigned for the prize and claimed to have settled eight wars, did not directly address Pillay's win; on Truth Social he reshared criticism of her.

What Happens Next

Rubio said the sanctions were structured to give the court and its member states a chance to address American concerns. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," he said. The administration's six-month wind-down window is, in the State Department's words, "intended to provide time" for diplomatic and legal resolutions — and can be adjusted depending on how those efforts go.

Whether Washington's allies comply or rally behind the court will decide how much of the damage the ICC can absorb. The EU's blocking mechanism, which has never been tested at this scale, is about to get its first real trial — and a court built to hold the powerful to account is about to find out whether its own members will hold the line.
